title: Axillary lump with no obvious breast lesion

header.contentArea: Assessment of axillary lymphadenopathy with possible occult breast primary
guidelineVersions: NICE NG101 Early and locally advanced breast cancer (current)

related.why: The examination technique extended here to the axilla in the absence of an obvious breast lump
A contrasting axillary presentation in a different clinical context

brief.scenario: Mrs Delgado, 55, has noticed a lump in her right armpit over the past month. She reports no breast lump on self-examination.
brief.task: Take a focused history to assess this axillary lump, including possible occult breast malignancy. You will be stopped at 6 minutes.

beforeYouWalkIn.frame: An axillary lump without an obvious breast lesion still requires careful breast-focused assessment, since an occult primary is an important cause not to miss.
beforeYouWalkIn.trap: Assuming the absence of a breast lump on self-examination excludes a breast primary, and focusing only on other causes of lymphadenopathy.
beforeYouWalkIn.firstMove: "Can you tell me more about the lump itself, and anything else you've noticed?"

flow: Screen for a breast primary despite no self-detected lump
Screen for other causes of lymphadenopathy (infection, skin, systemic)
At 6 minutes: present findings and differential

grid.label: Characterising the axillary lump
grid.fail: Does not establish onset, size change, or consistency of the lump.
grid.pass: Establishes onset, whether it has grown, and whether it feels hard, fixed or mobile.
grid.high: Uses these features to help judge how concerning the lump is (e.g. hard, fixed, enlarging nodes being more concerning than soft, mobile ones).

grid.label: Screening for a breast primary
grid.fail: Accepts that there's no breast lump at face value and moves on without further breast-focused questioning.
grid.pass: Asks specifically about any breast skin changes, nipple changes, or subtle symptoms she may not have recognised as significant.
grid.high: Explains that a breast primary can be too small to feel, or hidden in dense breast tissue, so a normal self-examination doesn't exclude it, and imaging is still needed.

grid.label: Alternative causes of lymphadenopathy
grid.fail: Does not consider or ask about other causes of axillary lymphadenopathy.
grid.pass: Asks about recent skin infections or injuries to the arm/hand, and any other lumps elsewhere (e.g. neck, groin).
grid.high: Considers a broader differential including infective, dermatological, and other malignant causes (e.g. lymphoma, melanoma) alongside occult breast cancer.

grid.label: Systemic symptoms
grid.fail: Does not screen for systemic symptoms.
grid.pass: Asks about fever, night sweats, weight loss and fatigue.
grid.high: Uses the presence or absence of systemic B symptoms to help weigh lymphoma against other causes in the differential.

grid.label: Presentation of findings
grid.fail: Concludes this is unlikely to be breast-related simply because she found no lump herself.
grid.pass: Presents a differential that includes occult breast malignancy alongside infective and other causes, without dismissing the breast as a source.
grid.high: Explicitly explains why occult breast primary remains an important differential despite a normal self-examination, avoiding false reassurance.

grid.label: Next steps
grid.fail: Recommends only observation or antibiotics without breast-specific imaging.
grid.pass: Recommends urgent triple assessment of the breast (including imaging) alongside assessment of the axillary node itself (ultrasound plus core biopsy), reflecting the NG12 referral threshold plus standard investigation practice.
grid.high: Explains that if breast imaging is normal, further investigation for other causes of lymphadenopathy, including lymphoma, would then be pursued.

failures.move: Moves straight into the differential or management plan without asking how long the lump has been present, whether it has changed, or how it feels.
failures.consequence: Without these features, the candidate cannot judge how concerning the node is or track relevant change over time.

failures.move: Does not ask about fever, night sweats, weight loss or fatigue.
failures.consequence: Missing systemic B symptoms means lymphoma cannot be properly weighed against other causes in the differential.

failures.move: Accepting a normal breast self-examination as excluding a breast primary.
failures.consequence: An occult breast primary can be small, deep, or in dense tissue and undetectable by self-examination, so this reasoning risks missing the diagnosis.

failures.move: Recommending watchful waiting without any breast imaging or axillary node assessment.
failures.consequence: Delays diagnosis and treatment of a potentially serious underlying cause, whether malignant or otherwise.

failures.move: Not considering alternative causes of axillary lymphadenopathy.
failures.consequence: Narrows the differential prematurely, risking a missed diagnosis such as lymphoma if breast causes are excluded.

recovery.when: You dismissed a breast cause due to normal self-examination
recovery.line: Let me reconsider - a breast primary can still be present even without a lump she's been able to feel.
Actually, given this is firm and enlarging, I should arrange proper investigation now rather than just observing.

knowledge.fact: An occult breast primary should be actively considered and investigated with breast imaging in a woman presenting with an axillary lymph node metastasis, even without a palpable breast lump.
A firm, enlarging axillary lymph node without an obvious infective cause warrants urgent assessment including ultrasound and core biopsy of the node itself, alongside breast imaging.
Other important causes of axillary lymphadenopathy to consider include infection (e.g. from a skin lesion on the arm or hand) and lymphoma, particularly when systemic B symptoms are present.

recall.think: No felt lump doesn't exclude a breast primary; assess the node and image the breast.
recall.say: "This doesn't exclude an occult breast cancer."

Arrange breast imaging plus axillary node ultrasound and biopsy

partner.opening: Please take a history from this patient about her axillary lump. I'll stop you at 6 minutes.
partner.actorBrief: You are Mrs Delgado, 55, with a one-month history of a firm, slightly enlarging right axillary lump. You have checked your breast carefully yourself and found nothing. No skin infections, no other lumps, no systemic symptoms.

reveals.trigger: Asks about subtle breast changes despite normal self-exam
reveals.finding: No skin, nipple or breast changes noticed.

reveals.trigger: Asks about infection or other lumps
reveals.finding: No recent skin infections, no other lumps elsewhere.
No fever, night sweats, weight loss or fatigue.

push.question: If I've checked my breast and found nothing, could it still be from there?
push.expect: Explain that a breast primary can be too small to feel or hidden in dense tissue, so imaging is still needed despite normal self-examination.

push.question: What tests will I need?
push.expect: Explain that both breast imaging and assessment of the axillary node (ultrasound and biopsy) will be arranged.

curveballs.prompt: I also noticed a small scratch on that arm from my cat a few weeks ago - could that be it?
curveballs.safeAnswer: Consider this as a possible contributing or alternative cause, but continue with full assessment rather than assuming it fully explains a firm, enlarging node.

curveballs.prompt: What if the breast scans come back completely normal?
curveballs.safeAnswer: Explain that if breast imaging is normal, further assessment for other causes of the node, including biopsy for lymphoma, would then be pursued.
